book: 159 - The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness

chapters.relation: Applies George Orwell's distinction between patriotism (defensive devotion open to critique) and nationalism (obsessive, unstable, indifferent to reality) to Belt politics, reading Drummer as the patriot — she works for the Earther Fred Johnson, turns her guns on Belter radicals in 'Pyre', and refuses to whitewash Marco's massacres ('We're scavengers') — and Marco Inaros as the nationalist, whose asteroid genocide, treatment of Naomi as a welwala, and brainwashing of Filip ('All I did, I did for all Belters') display obsession, loyalty-transfer, and indifference to reality. The chapter's twist is that by Season 5 the patriots lose, because nationalists can always outbid defenders who play only defense, so neither Drummer nor Marco has the right attitude; Avasarala's finale call to 'turn every Belter, Martian, and Earther into this [the Rocinante crew]' makes cosmopolitanism — shared humanity over national loyalty — the show's real answer.

chapters.file: ch25 - “I Want to Conquer the World”.md
chapters.relation: Uses Agamben's bios/zoē distinction (with Foucault on biopolitics and fragmented sovereignty, Hardt and Negri's 'Empire', Marx on surplus-value, and Rosa Luxemburg on unchecked capital) to read the Anderson Station massacre, Murtry shooting Coop on New Terra, and Protogen infecting 1.5 million Belters on Eros as reductions of Belter life to bare life that corporate sovereigns may kill without homicide. It then argues the instability capitalism creates births authoritarian sovereigns — Murtry's martial law, Inaros's Free Navy, Duarte's Laconia — whose followers (Chandra Wei, Cyn, Santiago Singh) display the 'total, unrestricted, unconditional loyalty' Arendt says totalitarian power demands, and closes with Foucault's warning that liberal government's security-for-freedom trade slides into the very corruption and oppression it was meant to prevent.

Reads Protogen through Horkheimer and Adorno's Dialectic of Enlightenment: like Odysseus tied to the mast while his sailors take the wax, Dresden's team had empathy surgically removed ('we modified our science team to remove ethical restraints'), Mao weeps at Julie's protomolecule corpse yet calls her death 'lucky', and Strickland experiments on Katoa and Mei Meng — self-made monsters serving the Baconian dream of conquering nature (New Atlantis, witch-trial language of 'penetrating her holes and corners'). Via Maria Mies and Carolyn Merchant's ecofeminism, it traces this domination of nature to pastoralist castration and the control of women's reproduction, culminating in Marco's theft of Filip and 'She left us. She left us both' — Naomi cast as nature to be mastered. Against them, Holden's childhood on the family farm, a cooperative 'let grow and make grow' world, is why Avasarala cannot play him and why he withholds broadcasts at Ilus: he is a knight who wants everyone to grow and speak for themselves, not to conquer.

chapters.file: ch27 - Fourth Orbit THEY STILL DREAM.md
ch28 - “Doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing”.md
chapters.relation: Reads The Expanse as a portrait of a survived-but-unlearned Anthropocene: Bobbie's mourning encounter with Earth's dead, walled ocean in 'Cascade', Prax Meng's cascade of cascading failures killing Ganymede's artificial ecosystem and manufacturing Belter climate refugees overnight, and the slum outside the UN gates where children drink sewer water. Drawing on Brian Henning's 'Technozoic' critique, Katie McShane, Keekok Lee's intrinsic value of inanimate nature, and Henry Shue and Kyle Whyte on climate justice and colonialism, it argues humanity simply exported its anthropocentric, colonial worldview to Mars terraforming, Ilus, and the Ring worlds instead of changing it — Belters standing in for the Global South — so the Roci's creed that 'doing nothing is just as bad as doing the wrong thing' becomes a demand for environmental justice and a non-anthropocentric ethics.

Tests the moral limits of science against Dresden's defense of Eros ('hardly a rounding error', 'we become our own gods'): Descartes' evil demon explains why Holden can never verify the protomolecule-ghost Miller — or even the Roci's bulkhead — is real; Baconian induction and mastery of nature explain why Protogen feeds biomass to the protomolecule ('we can only learn by letting it learn'), though Bacon himself demanded knowledge be shared for universal good; Peirce's pragmatism explains how the Donnager infers stealth ships from their effects and why protomolecule victims count as no longer human; and Dewey's inseparability of means and ends indicts Fred Johnson's readiness to negotiate with Dresden. It culminates in Miller shooting Dresden — 'I killed him because he was making sense' — as the straightest critique of utilitarian calculation, concluding that when empathy is excised (Cortázar's stimulation) or ignored, even science aimed at saving humanity produces Eros, Project Caliban, and the Earth-Mars war.

chapters.file: ch30 - It’s Life in the Solar System, Jim, But Not as We Know It.md
chapters.relation: Uses MacIntyre's demand for self-knowledge — awareness of the social and political currents that shape one's beliefs — to diagnose the Martian Congressional Republic's exceptionalism (Lopez berating 'short-sighted and selfish' Earthers from the Donnager) and to chart Bobbie Draper's redemption arc: refusing to fire first on Ganymede, refusing to bear false witness after the hearings, protecting Holden at the Ring Station, defecting to Avasarala, and finally rescuing Naomi. It maps MCR culture onto American space culture — Kennedy's Rice speech, the Mars Society and National Space Society founding statements, Zubrin's Case for Mars, and Patricia Limerick's and Linda Billings's critique of the 'conquering the space frontier' metaphor, with Carnap's frameworks and Kuhn's incommensurability explaining how metaphors hide alternatives — and argues the MCR never acquires self-knowledge, a failure that ends in its alliance with Marco Inaros and the move to Laconia, while Draper's willingness to update her beliefs shows what philosophy asks of real spaceflight advocates.

chapters.file: ch31 - Fifth Orbit TILTING AT WINDMILLS.md
ch32 - The Burden of the End of the World.md
chapters.relation: Reads Naomi's escape from collapsing Ganymede — sedating Amos to leave the freighter, then stepping out before a crowd of more than a hundred stranded Belters to propose saving only the youngest — as Arendt's 'doing' politics, action justified by the seeing-and-being-seen of shared speech rather than by the strategic 'making' calculus Melissa and Amos use to justify abandoning the crowd. Naomi must alternate between the two — Champa's measured violence organizes the crowd — without letting making become the ethical metric, because, as she says, 'every shitty thing we do makes the next one that much easier.' Marco embodies politics reduced to pure making (abandoning six million on Ceres), Holden stays trapped in righteous strategizing that never defeats the protomolecule's uncertainty, and the chapter closes on Arendt's story of Plato's philosopher-king: trying to eliminate uncertainty by preemptive rule only multiplies risk, so resilience comes from doing politics together.

chapters.file: ch33 - Knuckles and the Augustín Gamarra.md
chapters.relation: Deploys Crenshaw's intersectionality to explain why Naomi — the only Belter and only woman aboard the Rocinante — reads as a serial traitor: giving the protomolecule to Fred Johnson out of loyalty to the Belt, leaving Filip to escape Inaros's control of her through motherhood, and siding with Miller after the Dresden shooting ('as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong'). It scales the analysis up to Belters as a collectively intersectional group — race, class, refugee status, and colonial occupation at once, as with the Weeping Somnambulist fired on carrying 55 refugees and the Ilus colonists framed through the European conquest of the Americas — then walks through Naomi's past with Marco (the Augustín Gamarra bombing that killed 516 people, her suicide attempt, 'the right to walk away') to show that resisting intersecting oppressions forces impossible, betrayal-laden choices, with her chosen family on the Roci as a model of solidarity that crosses identity lines.

Maps conflicts between incommensurable kinds of value across the series: moral versus epistemic value in Dresden's 'we become our own gods' defense of Eros and Strickland's knowingly continued torture of children on Io; moral versus aesthetic value in Cortázar calling protomolecule-infected Julie 'beautiful' and Anna Volovodov ignoring Nemeroff's suicidal pleas on the Thomas Prince because she craves the sublime Ring; and epistemic versus prudential value in Iturbi and Janus losing the Arboghast and Okoye calling Holden's nightmares 'an acceptable tradeoff'. The chapter argues that because we can rarely be certain which value should govern, every such tradeoff is itself a moral risk — even a correct choice leaves a residue of sacrificed value, and Dresden's and Cortázar's certainty is reckless because unjustified — before weighing dilemma, permissibility, and ranking models and settling on pluralism, with Holden 'pushing buttons as we find them'.

chapters.file: ch35 - Sixth Orbit RIDING THE ROCI.md
ch36 - The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat.md
chapters.relation: Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.

Reads Naomi through Latina feminist phenomenology — Ortega's 'multiplicitous subjectivity', Lugones's 'world-traveling', Anzaldúa's borderlands — as one subject inhabiting several incompatible social worlds at once: Belter and Roci crewmate, Marco's former partner and Holden's lover, who experiences Miller's killing of Dresden simultaneously as her captain does and 'as a Belter, Miller wasn't wrong.' Du Bois's double consciousness names her two-ness when the Inaros faction pulls her back into a world she can still slip into 'as if she'd never stopped', and Ashford's list of her identities ('radical, betrayed, hid with the Inners, big hero') shows the borderlands Belters occupy between Inner and Outer worlds. The chapter argues this unsettlement is not a defect but a critical vantage: one stream of experience can carry multiple, conflicting meanings simultaneously, and all of it — no part more than another — is who Naomi is.

chapters.file: ch38 - On the Other Side of the Ring A Difficult Consequence.md
chapters.relation: Uses Wittgenstein's 'if a lion could talk, we would not understand him' and his shift from the Tractatus picture-book model to the Investigations' language-game model to explain why Inners and Belters, though they share a language, still cannot understand each other: 'Rocinante' and 'MCRN Tachi' name the same ship but mean differently, Earth plays the post-scarcity-superpower game around Basic assistance while Mars plays the driven-upstart game and the Belt the liberation game, and Holden's family's casual 'skinnies' slur shows even love cannot supply missing context. The chapter runs through Okoye's lab 'scalpel' joke and the use–mention distinction to make the model precise, then draws the dark consequence: understanding fails at every scale, from Avasarala versus Dawes to Bobbie versus the Laconians to humanity versus the Ring Builders and Unknown Aggressors ('Some of them are even playing the language game of genocide'), leaving Star Trek-style optimism naive and only the small, personal understandings — Naomi, Amos, Bobby — attainable.

holes.name: Patriotism vs Nationalism (Orwell's distinction)
holes.what: George Orwell's distinction between patriotism (defensive devotion to a place and way of life, forced on no one) and nationalism (obsessive identification that places the nation beyond good and evil in a quest for power).
holes.why: Chapter 24's entire reading of Drummer as patriot versus Marco Inaros as nationalist is built on this distinction and its three markers (obsession, instability, indifference to reality), which taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Contemporary Italian philosopher whose Homo Sacer analyzes sovereignty through bare life and the state of exception.
holes.why: Chapter 25 uses his bios/zoē distinction as its central tool for reading Belters as lives the sovereign 'is permitted to kill without committing homicide'.

holes.name: Bare Life (homo sacer, state of exception)
holes.what: Life excluded from the political and legal order, reduced to mere existence, that the sovereign may kill without committing homicide.
holes.why: Chapter 25 argues Belters at Anderson Station, on Ilus/New Terra, and on Eros are repeatedly reduced to bare life by corporate and political sovereigns.

holes.name: Biopolitics (power over life)
holes.what: Foucault's account of modern power that manages populations and decides whose life counts, blurring sovereignty across political, capitalist, and military actors.
holes.why: Chapter 25 frames the Anderson Station massacre and the Eros experiment through Foucault's Birth of Biopolitics and the fragmentation of sovereignty, themes taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Max Horkheimer
holes.what: Critical theorist who co-authored Dialectic of Enlightenment with Adorno, including the rereading of Odysseus and the Sirens as the first self-mastery in the domination of nature.
holes.why: Chapter 26 builds its portrait of Dresden, Mao, and Strickland as self-made monsters on Horkheimer and Adorno's Sirens episode and domination-of-nature thesis; Adorno is in taxonomy but Horkheimer is not.

holes.name: Domination of Nature
holes.what: The Enlightenment dream (Bacon onward, reinterpreted by Horkheimer/Adorno and ecofeminists like Mies and Merchant) of boundless mastery over nature, which extends to the domination of women and the self.
holes.why: Chapter 26 reads Protogen's experiments and Marco's control of Naomi's reproduction through this thesis, and contrasts Holden's 'let grow and make grow' farm with it.

holes.name: The Anthropocene
holes.what: The proposed geological epoch in which human activity is the dominant force shaping Earth's climate and ecosystems, and the debates (anthropocentrism, Technozoic fixes, climate justice) around it.
holes.why: Chapter 28 is organized entirely around the Anthropocene — Earth's paved garden, Ganymede's cascade, Belter climate refugees — and taxonomy.json has no slug for it.

holes.name: The Frontier Myth and American Exceptionalism
holes.what: The destiny narrative casting space as a frontier to be conquered, importing American exceptionalist rhetoric into spaceflight culture (Kennedy, Mars Society, Zubrin).
holes.why: Chapter 30 argues the MCR's Martian exceptionalism is a direct import of this frontier rhetoric and that its unexamined metaphors block the MacIntyrean self-knowledge the chapter advocates.

holes.name: Politics as Action: Making vs Doing
holes.what: Arendt's Human Condition distinction between making politics (strategic control of outcomes) and doing politics (speech and action that build a common world no one controls).
holes.why: Chapter 32's organizing argument is that Naomi's Ganymede rescue is doing politics balanced against Amos's and Melissa's making, a distinction taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Value Pluralism and Incommensurability
holes.what: The view that moral, epistemic, aesthetic, and prudential values are irreducible kinds sharing no common currency, whose conflicts may be dilemmas, matters of permissibility, or resolvable rankings.
holes.why: Chapter 34's entire argument about risky tradeoffs (Dresden, Cortázar, Volovodov, Okoye) rests on conflicts between incommensurable kinds of value, which taxonomy.json lacks.

holes.name: Multiplicitous Subjectivity and World-Traveling
holes.what: Latina feminist phenomenology (Ortega, Lugones, Anzaldúa) of selves who inhabit several overlapping social worlds at once and travel between them, experiencing conflicting meanings simultaneously.
holes.why: Chapter 37 applies it directly to Naomi's life between Belter and Roci worlds, using Du Bois's double consciousness (which is in taxonomy) as its ancestor but lacking the central concept itself.
